All cyclic voltammetry experiments were performed using a 3-electrode set-up with a 3 mm glassy carbon working electrode, a platinum wire counter electrode and \mathrm { A g / A g N O _ { 3 } } reference electrode. Prior to measurement the working electrode was polished with 0.05 µm polishing power and the platinum counter electrode was flame dried. Tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate (TBAPF<sub>6</sub>) electrolyte was recrystallized in ethanol and dried under vacuum in an oil bath ( 7 0 ^ { \mathrm { { o } } } \mathrm { C } ) to ensure purity. To a flame-dried vial was added 0.1 M \mathrm { T B A P F } _ { 6 } in MeCN and substrate (2.5 mM). The vial headspace was purged with nitrogen gas for two minutes prior to scanning in the anodic direction ( 0 \mathrm { V { \stackrel { - } { \to } } 1 . 3 \ o r \ } . 4 \mathrm { V } \to 0 \mathrm { V } ) . Each sample was charged with solid ferrocene (1-4 mg) and calibrated to the Fc/Fc+ reference potential.

To a flame-dried vial was added substrate (5.0 mM) in 0.1 M \mathrm { T B A P F } _ { 6 } in MeCN. The vial headspace was purged with nitrogen for two minutes prior to scanning in the anodic direction and the potential windows were set to 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ - ~ } 1 . 3 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } ( \mathbf { S 1 } ) or 0 ~ \mathrm { V } - 1 . 4 ~ \bar { \mathrm { V } } ~ ( \mathbf { S 9 } ) . All yields and data provided are crude results relative to mesitylene internal standard. Products are identified either through comparison of known products or best assigned based on similar materials in literature. Experiments were conducted during multiple points during optimization campaign hence the varied reaction conditions.

A 5 mL electrasyn vial was charged with alkoxyamine substrate (0.3 mmol, 1 equiv), nucleophile (0.9 mmol, 3.0 equiv), 2,4,6-trimethylpyridine (79.4 µL, 0.6 mmol, 2.0 equiv), tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate (116 mg, 0.3 mmol, 1.0 equiv), deionized water (50 \mu \mathrm { L } ) , and anhydrous MeCN (3.0 mL). The mixture was stirred until obtaining a homogenous solution, the cap was assembled with platinum and graphite electrodes, and the solution was electrolyzed (i = 15 mA, 13 F/mol, 1200 RPM; or 6 hr 58 min constant current electrolysis). Following electrolysis, the mixture was concentrated in vacuo removing MeCN. Crude <sup>1</sup>H NMR was conducted using mesitylene as internal standard (10 µL, 215.6 µmol C–H aromatic proton integration). The mixture was diluted with EtOAc (~30 mL) and was washed with 1x saturated NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (~30 mL), 1x HCl (1.0 M; or saturated NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, ~30 mL), 1x saturated brine (~30 mL), and dried by flowing the solution through a plug of solid anhydrous \mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } . The crude residue was purified by column chromatography using EtOAc in hexanes to furnish the desired products. Notes:

A 10 mL electrasyn vial was charged with alkoxyamine substrate S1 (289 mg, 1.0 mmol, 1 equiv), benzoic acid (366 mg, 3.0 mmol, 3.0 equiv), 2,4,6-trimethylpyridine (264 µL, 2.0 mmol, 2.0 equiv), tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate (194 mg, 0.5 mmol, 0.5equiv), deionized water (167 µL, 9.25 mmol, 9.25 equiv), and anhydrous MeCN (5.0 mL). The mixture was stirred until obtaining a homogenous solution, the cap was assembled with platinum and graphite electrodes, and the solution was electrolyzed (i = 15 mA, 9 F/mol, 1200 RPM). Following electrolysis, the mixture was concentrated in vacuo removing MeCN. Crude <sup>1</sup>H NMR was conducted using mesitylene as internal standard returning 80% yield (20 µL, 431.2 µmol C–H aromatic proton integration). The mixture was diluted with EtOAc (~50 mL) and was washed with 2x saturated NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (~40 mL), 2x HCl (1.0 M, ~30 mL), 1x saturated brine (~40 mL), and dried by flowing the solution through a plug of solid anhydrous { \mathrm { N a } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { S O } } _ { 4 } . The crude residue was added to silica gel and the solvent was removed. Flash chromatography using a Biotage (50 g silica, 0→12% EtOAc/hexanes over 12 column volumes) afforded the desired product 1 as a white solid (203 mg, 80%) with spectral properties consistent with benzoate data yielded in section 7.3.

Ground-state conformations of the anodically generated radical cations of S1, S3, S5, S6, S7, S8, and S19 were obtained using the conformational search tool in Rowan Scientific employing the CREST method in “careful” mode. Conformers within 5.0 kcal/mol energy difference from the lowest energy conformer were subjected to gas-phase geometry optimizations using the B3LYP functional and 6 { \cdot } 3 1 1 \mathrm { G } ( \mathsf { d } , \mathsf { p } ) basis set phase in Gaussian 16. Unscaled harmonic frequency calculations at the same level were performed to validate each structure as a minimum and to evaluate their zero-point energies and thermal corrections at 1 atm and 298 K. Single point energy refinements were performed at the SMD/B3LYP/6-311G(d,p) level to obtain solvation free energies in acetonitrile (MeCN) in addition to NBO calculated parameters. Discussed energy differences are based on Gibbs free energies in solution.

The lowest energy conformation for { \displaystyle { \bf S } } { \bf 5 } ^ { + } { \bf \cdot } is illustrated in the figure below. A notable structural feature is the alignment of the N5–O4 and \mathrm { C } 2 { = } \mathrm { O } 1 bonds, forming a 5-membered complex to effectively delocalize the spin density along the substrate backbone. The ground state conformers of { \bf S } 3 ^ { + } ; { \bf S } 7 ^ { + } . and { \bf S 8 ^ { + } } <sup>.</sup> were found to also adopt this complexed configuration. In contrast, due to steric encumbrance induced by the butyl-side chain, complexation in \mathbf { S 6 ^ { + } } is disfavored (see \mathbf { S 6 } ^ { + } { \cdot } { \mathbf { c } } 2 , + 2 . 5 kcal/mol). Instead, \mathbf { S 6 ^ { + } { - } c 1 } adopts a distal conformation where the spin density is highly localized on the N5-center. We postulate that poor reactivity and irreversible electrochemical profile observed for S6 may be attributed to decomposition of \mathbf { S 6 ^ { + } } via 1,5 or 1,6–hydrogen atom abstraction along the butyl sidechain. This is further evidenced by the isolation of cyclized products early during the optimization campaign using substrates 4- phenyl-1-(pyrrolidin-1-yl)-2-((2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-yl)oxy)butan-1-one or 1- (pyrrolidin-1-yl)-2-((2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-yl)oxy)hexan-1-one.

The energetically disfavored conformation \mathbf { S 6 ^ { + } { - } c 2 } is also shown.

We performed NBO analysis of the geometry optimized radical cations to probe the origin of substituent effects. The table below shows the calculated NBO charges, energies and occupancies of the C–OTMP bond (C3–O4). Substrates with more positive NBO charges on C3 exhibit more facile oxidation potentials and higher overall yields. This is also observed for increasing negative character on O4, suggesting that a more polarized, therefore weaker, C3– O4 bond is more susceptible to nucleophilic attack. Gratifyingly, the calculated NBO C3–O4 bond energy was found to be moderately predictive of reaction success. Through this analysis we may rationalize synthetic reactivity trends, such as the rate decrease seen upon varying the heteroatom from amide S5 -> methyl ester S3 -> carboxylic acid S8. Less polarization, therefore increased stability, of the C3–O4 bond may also explain why primary alkoxyamines are challenging to activate S19, which is further evidenced by its \mathrm { E } _ { 1 / 2 } and low reaction yield.

ABSTRACT: The reactivity and synthetic utility of TEMPOderived alkoxyamines as functional handles remains insuficiently explored. This report interrogates the factors governing the stereospecific substitution of electroactivated TEMPO-derived α- carbonyl alkoxyamines. Concurrent with direct electrolysis, electroanalytical studies and theoretical calculations provided a complementary platform by which one could predict the eficacy for substrates to undergo desired substitution using benzoic acid or N-sulfonyl carbamate nucleophiles.

We selected propiophenone-derived alkoxyamine S1 as our model substrate (Figure 2A). Preliminary CV analysis displayed an oxidative profile consistent with an EC mechanism ( \mathrm { i . e . , ~ a ~ } coupled sequence of an electron transfer step (E) followed by a chemical reaction step (C)), where S1 can be oxidized and reduced quasi-reversibly<sup>26</sup> with a prominent return peak showing the reduction of the singly oxidized radical cation ( \mathbf { S _ { l } } ^ { \bullet + } ; i _ { \mathrm { c } } / i _ { \mathrm { a } } = 0 . 6 0 ) . This result indicates that \mathbf { S 1 ^ { \bullet + } } is relatively stable so that direct S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2 may be possible upon electrochemical activation. However, the presence of a small TEMPO<sup>+</sup> reduction peak (peak potential E _ { \mathrm { p } } \sim + 0 . 3 \ : \mathrm { V } vs Fc/Fc<sup>+</sup>) indicates that \hat { \mathbf { s 1 ^ { \bullet + } } } undergoes slow unproductive mesolytic cleavage.

Guided by our voltammetry data, we first explored the benzoyloxylation of propiophenone (S1) with α-TEMPO substitution (Figure 2B). After optimization, we found substitution proceeded smoothly in an undivided cell employing a graphite anode and platinum cathode, three equivalents of benzoic acid nucleophile with two equivalents of ^ { 2 , 4 , 6 - } colidine as the base, tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate as the electrolyte, and dry acetonitrile (MeCN) as the solvent with 50 μL of water added as a sacrificial proton source (entry 1).

With these optimized conditions in hand, we then assessed various TEMPO-substituted carbonyl electrophiles through electrolysis experiments and CV analysis. First, by conducing the reaction at a higher concentration, we achieved a 1 mmol scale electrolysis using model substrate S1 with no compromise in yield while improving the faradaic eficiency (see SI section 7.2). Cyclic secondary amide S2 was compatible with optimal conditions without the need for an N-protecting group. DCM was found to be an efective alternative solvent in this case, providing similar yield with lower equivalents of electron input and base required. Acyclic ester S3 and tertiary amide S4 were also converted to the desired products (3 and 4, respectively) in moderate to good yield (Figure 3A). Analogous to S1, S2−S4 displayed reversible CV profiles,<sup>26</sup> with low degrees of mesolytic cleavage observed (Figure 3B).

Unexpectedly, we found that substrates derived from Weinreb amides (S5 and S6) display disparate activities: propionic acid-derived S5 underwent desired transformation to yield 44% of product 5, whereas hexanoic acid-derived S6 returned no desired product. To understand these findings, we compared the voltammetric behaviors of S5 and S6 (Figure 3C). S5 bearing the methyl side chain exhibited a largely reversible electrochemical behavior with a minor degree of mesolytic cleavage. In contrast, S6 displayed a completely irreversible voltammogram but also showed no sign of TEMPO<sup>+</sup> reduction that would result from mesolytic cleavage. Supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we hypothesize that upon oxidation of the aminoxyl substituent to a radical cation, unproductive intramolecular HAT took place (possibly 1,5-HAT), leading to side reactivities instead of desired substitution (see SI section 10.2).

Analogously, when conducting electrolysis experiments using aldehyde- and carboxylic acid-derived alkoxyamines (S7 and S8), no desired products were detected. From CV analysis, we observed that substrates S7 and S8 displayed irreversible profiles with a pronounced return peak corresponding to TEMPO<sup>+</sup> reduction (see SI section 3.2). Thus, we posit that radical cation intermediates bearing aldehyde or carboxylic acid groups are inherently unstable where mesolytic cleavage occurs rapidly after oxidation to furnish an α-carbonyl radical.

It should be noted primary alkoxyamines are not amenable to substitution under the optimal reaction conditions. Ethyl acetate- and acetophenone-derived (S14) alkoxyamines, though exhibiting fully reversible CV profiles with little to no apparent mesolytic cleavage, return low yields (see SI section 5.1). DFT calculations indicated the C−OTMP bond strength of S14<sup>•+</sup> is significantly stronger than its secondary counterpart (S1<sup>•+</sup>). In addition, we found that the C−OTMP bond in { \hat { \mathbf { s } } } \mathbf { 1 } ^ { \bullet + } is substantially polarized with a partial positive natural bond orbital (NBO) charge (+0.062) at the α-carbon, which favors nucleophilic substitution. In stark contrast, the α-carbon in S14<sup>•+</sup> bears a significant partial negative NBO charge (−0.10), which likely deters substitution at this position (see SI section 10.3). Sterics likely has a negligible influence in this case, as it was previous found that the rate of S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2 adjacent to a carbonyl group is insensitive to the size of the substituent at the α- carbon. 27

To further probe our proposed S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2 mechanism, we prepared a set of diastereomeric substrates. trans-Cyclohexanone S9 aforded exclusively cis-cyclohexanone 9. Interestingly, cisdiastereomer S10 displayed poor reactivity toward substitution due to a lack of stereoelectronic stabilization of the S _ { \mathrm { N } } 2 transition state and the intrinsic dificulty of displacing an equatorial substituent.<sup>27,28</sup> Nonetheless, only the transbenzoyloxylation product 10 was observed. The voltammetry behaviors of S9 and S10 were also recorded (Figure 3D). Cyclohexanone S9 exhibits a substantial degree of mesolytic cleavage at a scan rate of 250 mV/s or lower, but with a faster scan rate cleavage is lessened (see SI section 3.2). Thus, upon single-electron oxidation, { \bf 5 9 } ^ { \bullet + } is primed for direct substitution, but the radical cation intermediate is relatively short-lived. Using a method similar to that of Sigman and Minteer et al., cyclic voltammetry was employed to determine relative mesolytic cleavage rates, revealing that \mathbf { S 9 } ^ { \bullet + } exhibits a rate of C−O cleavage nearly four times that of model system \mathbf { S 1 ^ { \bullet + } } (Figure 3E). In comparison, S10 exhibited little mesolytic cleavage under equivalent conditions, reflecting its stability likely because of the absence of hyperconjugation with the carbonyl group to help stabilize the C−O breaking transition state. 27,29

For cyclic lactones S11 and S12, both diastereomers exclusively returned the stereochemically inverted products in moderate to good yield, further indicating that direct bimolecular substitution is the predominant reaction pathway. Lastly, alkoxyamine S13, derived from a chiral oxazolidinone auxiliary, was readily substituted in 70% yield, which may be further derivatized toward diverse enantioenriched ester products. Taken together, the stereospecific reactivity observed with S9−S13�which encompass compounds with various carbonyl functionalities and skeletal arrangements�is consistent with a bimolecular substitution pathway.
